name: Kannada
signature: Rounded and looping like Telugu (its sister script), most letters topped by a small curved headstroke; no continuous top line.
notes: Syllabary generated from Unicode by generate_syllabary.py: each syllable is a base consonant (varga order) composed with a core vowel sign. Romanization is ISO-15919. The independent (word-initial) vowels are in `independentVowels`; the script's own digits are in `digits`. Stroke order is a separate, source-gated effort: only source-verified entries carry it, beginning with independent short a ಅ. Parts, not the grid: handwriting is authored only for independent vowels, base consonants (the entries with a single `components` line), and vowel signs; a syllable's figure is assembled from its parts and is never authored separately. When `penLifts` is absent it means NOT VERIFIED — never none — and must never be inferred from the length of `strokeOrder`.

strokeOrder: start at the upper left and go down the left side and round the base
without lifting, climb the right side and close the bowl leftward along the top
lift, then draw the lower bar from left to right
lift, then draw the short link up from the lower bar
lift, then draw the upper bar from left to right
without lifting, curl up into the hook
letters.strokeOrderNote: Six visible movements in four pen-down runs: the round bowl, the lower bar, the short link rising from it, and the upper bar with its hook, separated by three lifts.

strokeOrderSource.citation: Gopala Krishna A, Kannada-alphabet-ka.gif, animation of Kannada consonant ಕ, 44 frames, 4.4 seconds (Wikimedia Commons, 25 May 2016)
strokeOrderSource.variation: The CC BY-SA 4.0 animation writes ಕ in four pen-down runs: the round bowl from its upper left, counterclockwise (frames 0–14); after a lift, the lower bar from left to right (frames 15–18); after a second lift, the short link rising from that bar (frames 19–20); after a third lift, the upper bar from left to right curling up into the hook (frames 21–29). The frames were read from a mirror copy that matches the Commons file's listed size (245×192) and frame count. The path is fitted to the bundled Noto Sans Kannada outline rather than copying the animation's handwritten proportions; the animation's link bulges a little to the right, while that outline draws it as a straight waist, which the path follows, and the bowl's top is fused into the lower bar, so the closing movement runs along the lower part of that ink. The three-lift order remains the same.

strokeOrder: start at the curled tip inside the head and loop up over it clockwise

without lifting, drop from the point round the right lobe's base

letters.strokeOrderNote: The source shows eight movements in four pen-down runs; Omniglot's non-native copyists most often draw ಚ in two strokes (55%, 11 of 20). This ductus follows the eight movements in order and direction, lifting only before the upper bar: after the body the pen runs back along the lower bar, draws it, and comes back to climb the short link, ten movements in two runs.

strokeOrderSource.citation: Gopala Krishna A, Kannada-alphabet-cha.gif, animation of Kannada consonant ಚ, 52 frames, 5.2 seconds (Wikimedia Commons, 25 May 2016)
strokeOrderSource.variation: The CC BY-SA 4.0 animation writes ಚ in four pen-down runs: from the curled tip inside the head the pen loops up over the head clockwise, slants down to the left, rounds the left lobe and rises into the middle point, drops round the right lobe and climbs the right side, curving over at the top (frames 0–20); after a lift, the lower bar from left to right (frames 24–28); after a second lift, the short link rising from that bar (frame 31); after a third lift, the upper bar from left to right curling up into the hook (frames 34–39). Its body is ಬ's and its bars are ಕ's. The frames were read from a mirror copy (206×180, 52 frames); no listed size for the Commons file was available to compare it with, so only the slug and the frames were checked. The path is fitted to the bundled Noto Sans Kannada outline rather than copying the animation's handwritten proportions; in that outline the head's curled tip is a short wedge, where the path starts, and the right side runs up into the lower bar instead of curving over, so the climb ends at the bar. These runs stage the letter one part at a time; they are not a count of how often fluent writers lift the pen, and no native writers' pen data for Kannada was available. Omniglot (Lake, Salakhutdinov & Tenenbaum, Science 350:1332, 2015; https://github.com/brendenlake/omniglot, MIT licence) holds 20 drawings of ಚ, each by a different Amazon Mechanical Turk worker copying a printed exemplar online. They are non-native copyists, not native writers; where the same dataset can be set beside native writers' pen data (HP Labs India's Devanagari and Bangla sets), the copyists use more strokes than those writers, so their counts are read here only as a ceiling on native lifts, and only counts and shares are cited. Even under that ceiling, 55% of them (11 of 20) draw ಚ in two strokes and 15% (3 of 20) in one; 10% (2 of 20) use the animation's four. Those counts say how many strokes, not where they break, so this learner path keeps every run's order, start and direction as a segment and joins the first three runs, running back along the lower bar before drawing it and coming back to the link's foot after it, so the pen lifts once, before the upper bar.

compositionSource.citation: The Unicode Consortium, The Unicode Standard, Version 17.0, Core Specification, §12.8.2 ‘Principles of the Kannada Script’, U+0CCD KANNADA SIGN VIRAMA (2025)
compositionSource.variation: The standard identifies U+0CCD as Kannada's halant, virama, or vowel-omission sign; defines a dead consonant as consonant plus halant; and explains that the full consonant's horn is replaced by the bound halant sign. Section 12.8.3 further explains that such dead consonants normally combine with later consonants into conjuncts. Unicode specifies encoded composition and rendering behavior, not a universal handwriting direction or pen-lift count; the carrier-first instruction is therefore a transparent learner composition convention, and this entry deliberately makes no standalone ductus claim.
